mainTopic: שבועת העדות: who it applies to; the source that witnesses are men; fair treatment of litigants in court
overview: This amud opens the פרק of שבועת העדות. The משנה teaches that the oath only applies to people fit to testify: men and not women, non-relatives and not relatives, and כשרים and not פסולים. רבי מאיר and חכמים argue about whether a denial outside בית דין makes the witnesses liable. Witnesses who knew the testimony and swore falsely bring a קרבן עולה ויורד. The גמרא asks for the source that women do not testify. It brings three ברייתות that read ״ועמדו שני האנשים״ as speaking about עדים. Each ברייתא gives its own first proof and backs it up with a גזירה שוה from ״שני עדים״. Next, a ברייתא learns from the same פסוק that בעלי דינין should stand, and רבי יהודה says the real rule is equal treatment. ״בצדק תשפוט עמיתך״ teaches equal treatment in court and judging others לכף זכות. רב יוסף adds that a fellow in תורה and מצוות should be judged 'nicely.' The story of רב עולא's case before רב נחמן shows this means hearing his case first, not favoring him.

steps.title: Who the oath of testimony applies to
steps.stepSummary: The משנה teaches that שבועת העדות only applies to people who are fit to be witnesses: men, non-relatives, and כשרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The oath of testimony applies to men but not to women, to non-relatives but not to relatives, and to people who are fit to testify but not to people who are disqualified. The rule is that it only applies to people who are fit to testify.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens the topic of שבועת העדות by telling us whose false oath counts. Only someone who could actually testify in בית דין can be liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שבועת העדות is when a person swears that he does not know testimony for someone, but he really does know it. If his testimony would not have been accepted anyway, his denial caused no loss, so the oath does not apply to him. That is why the משנה closes with the general rule: only those fit to testify.

keyTerms.meaning: The oath of testimony: falsely swearing that you know no testimony
Relatives, who may not testify for or against family
People disqualified from testifying, for example because of sins they committed

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule sets up the גמרא's first question: where do we learn that women are not valid witnesses?

phrases.english: MISHNA: The oath of testimony
applies to men but not to women,
to non-relatives but not to relatives,
phrases.notes: Relatives of the people in the case, since they can't testify for them.

phrases.english: to those who are fit but not to those who are disqualified;
and it applies only to those fit to testify.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ שְׁבוּעַת הָעֵדוּת נוֹהֶגֶת בַּאֲנָשִׁים וְלֹא בְּנָשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opening of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שבועת העדות only applies to those fit to testify: men, non-relatives, and כשרים.

steps.title: Denying in court or outside court
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר and חכמים argue about whether witnesses who deny outside בית דין are liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבי מאיר, if the witness swears himself, he is liable whether he is in front of בית דין or not. If others make him swear, the witnesses are not liable until they deny it in בית דין. חכמים say that in both cases, whether he swore himself or others made him swear, they are only liable if they deny it in בית דין.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a מחלוקת about where the denial has to happen for the witnesses to be liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר splits the case. If the witness says the oath with his own mouth, he is liable even outside בית דין. If the oath is put on him by others, he is only liable when he denies in בית דין. חכמים make no split: liability always needs a denial in בית דין.

keyTerms.meaning: From his own mouth: he says the oath himself
From the mouth of others: someone else makes him swear

steps.confusionAlert: The opening words "in front of בית דין and not in front of בית דין" belong with "from his own mouth". They describe the case where he swears himself, and that is רבי מאיר's view.

phrases.aramaic: בִּפְנֵי בֵּית דִּין וְשֶׁלֹּא בִּפְנֵי בֵּית דִּין –
phrases.english: In front of a court and not in front of a court
when it is from his own mouth;
phrases.notes: He says the oath himself, so he is liable in either place.

phrases.english: but when it is from the mouth of others,

phrases.aramaic: אֵין חַיָּיבִין עַד שֶׁיִּכְפְּרוּ בָּהֶן בְּבֵית דִּין.
phrases.english: they are not liable until they deny it in court.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And the Sages say:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין מִפִּי עַצְמוֹ וּבֵין מִפִּי אֲחֵרִים –
phrases.english: Whether from his own mouth or from the mouth of others,

phrases.aramaic: אֵינָן חַיָּיבִין עַד שֶׁיִּכְפְּרוּ בָּהֶן בְּבֵית דִּין.
phrases.english: they are not liable until they deny it in court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with a new rule about where the denial happens
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: if he swore himself, he is liable even outside בית דין. חכמים: liability always requires a denial in בית דין.

steps.title: Intentional versus unwitting, and the offering
steps.stepSummary: Witnesses are liable if they knew the testimony, even if they did not know about the punishment. They bring a קרבן עולה ויורד.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are liable if they swore falsely on purpose. They are also liable if they did not know the oath carries liability, as long as they knew the testimony. They are not liable if they really did not know the testimony. What do they bring for swearing on purpose? A sliding-scale offering.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains which kind of knowing makes the witnesses liable, and what קרבן they bring.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two things a witness can know or not know: the oath's liability and the testimony itself. Knowing the testimony is the key. If he knew it, he is liable even if he did not know the oath's liability. If he honestly did not know the testimony, he is not liable. Unusually, even a deliberate false oath here brings a קרבן, the קרבן עולה ויורד.

keyTerms.meaning: A sliding-scale offering: its cost depends on what the person can afford

steps.whatToRemember: Witnesses are liable only if they really knew the testimony. Even for a deliberate false oath they bring a קרבן עולה ויורד.
steps.whyThisMatters: Normally a קרבן is only for mistakes. שבועת העדות is an exception, because a קרבן is brought even for doing it on purpose.

phrases.english: And they are liable for an intentional oath,
and for an unwitting oath together with intentional testimony,
phrases.notes: He didn't know swearing carries liability, but he did know he had testimony.

phrases.english: but they are not liable for it being unwitting.
phrases.notes: Here "unwitting" means he honestly didn't know the testimony.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה הֵן חַיָּיבִין עַל זְדוֹן הַשְּׁבוּעָה?
phrases.english: And what are they liable for an intentional oath?
A sliding-scale offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the משנה with the rules of intent and the קרבן
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Liability depends on knowing the testimony. The punishment is a קרבן עולה ויורד, even when the oath was intentional.

steps.title: Where do we learn this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that women are not included in שבועת העדות, since they are not valid witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: From where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by asking for the source of the משנה's first rule, that the oath applies to men and not women. This sets up the next step, which brings the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה stated that women are excluded without giving a reason. The גמרא wants the source in the תורה that only men serve as witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה
From where do we know these things?

phrases.english: GEMARA: From where are these matters derived?
phrases.notes: He is asking about the משנה's first rule, that women are left out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the משנה's first rule
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that women are not valid witnesses, and so are not included in שבועת העדות

steps.title: The verse about the two men
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads ״ועמדו שני האנשים״ as speaking about the witnesses, which shows that witnesses are men.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the Rabbis taught: "And the two men shall stand." The verse is speaking about witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by quoting a ברייתא. The ברייתא reads the פסוק's word "men" as describing the witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says "the two men shall stand" in a section about witnesses. If those "two men" are the witnesses, then the תורה is describing witnesses as men. That is the source that women do not serve as witnesses.

phrases.english: As the Rabbis taught:
"And the two men shall stand"
the verse is speaking about witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4 with a ברייתא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק ״ועמדו שני האנשים״ is about witnesses, so witnesses must be men.

steps.title: The litigants are already mentioned, so the two men must be the witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks whether ״שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ might mean the בעלי דינין. It answers that the בעלי דינין are already mentioned in the words ״אֲשֶׁר לָהֶם הָרִיב״, so ״שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ must be the עדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: You say the verse is about witnesses, but maybe it is about the litigants? Since the verse already says 'those who have the dispute,' the litigants are already mentioned. So what does 'the two men shall stand' mean? It must be talking about the witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא tests its own claim. Could ״שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ mean the two people in the court case? It then proves the answer is no.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק has two parts: ״שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ and ״אֲשֶׁר לָהֶם הָרִיב״. The second part clearly means the בעלי דינין. If the first part also meant them, the פסוק would be saying the same thing twice. So the first part must mean someone else: the עדים.

keyTerms.meaning: The litigants, the people who have the court case
So how do I explain (this word or phrase)?

phrases.english: You say it is about witnesses,
or perhaps it is only about the litigants?
When it says "between whom the controversy is,"
the litigants are already mentioned;

phrases.aramaic: הָא מָה אֲנִי מְקַיֵּים ״וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״?
phrases.english: so how do I explain "then the two men shall stand"?
The verse is speaking about witnesses.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר בְּעֵדִים, אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּבַעֲלֵי דִינִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from Step 5 and gives the proof for its reading.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The separate phrase ״אֲשֶׁר לָהֶם הָרִיב״ in דברים 19:17 already covers the בעלי דינין

steps.title: Backup proof: the word 'two' links to 'two witnesses'
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds a second proof, a גזירה שוה. The word ״שְׁנֵי״ in this פסוק matches ״שְׁנֵי עֵדִים״ two verses earlier. Just as that פסוק is about עדים, so is this one.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you are not convinced: it says 'two' here and it says 'two' there. Just as there it is about witnesses, here too it is about witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a backup proof in case the first one does not convince you.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גזירה שוה connects two פסוקים that share a word. Here the shared word is ״שְׁנֵי״. The other פסוק, ״עַל פִּי שְׁנֵי עֵדִים״, is clearly about עדים, so our פסוק must be about עדים too.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want to argue otherwise (introduces a backup proof)
Learning one פסוק from another because they share the same word

phrases.english: And if you wish to say otherwise:
it is stated here "two,"
and it is stated there "two";
just as there it is about witnesses,
so too here it is about witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, independent proof for the same conclusion.
steps.raayaSupportSource: גזירה שוה of ״שְׁנֵי״ with ״עַל פִּי שְׁנֵי עֵדִים״ (דברים 19:15)

steps.title: Why was a backup proof needed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what ״אִם נַפְשְׁךָ לוֹמַר״ means. Why wasn't the first proof enough?
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'if you wish to say' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up its next move. It wants to know what was weak about the first proof that the ברייתא needed a second one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא only adds a backup proof if someone could question the first one. The גמרא asks what that question could be.

phrases.english: What is meant by "if you wish to say"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks why the backup proof in Step 7 was needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What weakness in the first proof made the backup necessary

steps.title: The verse lacks 'and', so it might be about litigants the whole way through
steps.stepSummary: Someone could argue: the פסוק does not say ״וַאֲשֶׁר לָהֶם הָרִיב״ (with 'and'). So both phrases could describe the same people, the בעלי דינין. That is why the ברייתא adds the גזירה שוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you would say: since the verse does not write 'AND those who have the dispute,' the whole verse is talking about the litigants. That is why it says: 'two' here and 'two' there. Just as there it is about witnesses, here too it is about witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the weak spot in the first proof, and shows that the גזירה שוה fixes it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the letter 'and', ״אֲשֶׁר לָהֶם הָרִיב״ might simply describe ״שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״: 'the two men, the ones who have the dispute.' Then the whole פסוק would be about בעלי דינין, and the first proof falls away. The גזירה שוה does not depend on that wording, so it still works.
steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether the בעלי דינין are in the פסוק at all. The question is whether the 'two men' are a separate group or the same people.

phrases.english: And if you would say:
since it did not write "AND those between whom the controversy is,"
phrases.notes: With an 'and', it would clearly be a second group standing alongside the two men. Without it, it could be describing those same two men.

phrases.english: the whole verse is speaking about litigants;
therefore: it is stated here "two" and it is stated there "two";

phrases.aramaic: מָה לְהַלָּן בְּעֵדִים אַף כָּאן בְּעֵדִים.
phrases.english: just as there it is about witnesses, so too here it is about witnesses.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: מִדְּלָא כְּתִב ״וַאֲשֶׁר לָהֶם הָרִיב״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 8 by naming the weakness in the first proof.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because ״אֲשֶׁר לָהֶם הָרִיב״ has no 'and', the whole פסוק might be about בעלי דינין, so the גזירה שוה is needed.

steps.title: Second ברייתא: litigants can be more than two, so the 'two' must be witnesses
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא also says ״שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ means עדים. Its proof is different: if it meant בעלי דינין, why say 'two'? Court cases can have three litigants too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: 'Then the two men shall stand' is about witnesses. You say it is about witnesses, but maybe it is about the litigants? Would you really say that? Do only two people come to court, and three never come to court?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא. It reaches the same conclusion with a different first proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The number 'two' does not fit litigants, because a case can involve more than two people. The number does fit עדים, since two is the standard number of witnesses. So the פסוק must be about עדים.

keyTerms.meaning: You said (that)?! An expression of surprise

phrases.english: It is taught in another ברייתא:
"Then the two men shall stand":
the verse is speaking about witnesses.
You say it is about witnesses,
or perhaps it is only about the litigants?
Would you really say that?
Do two people come to court,
but three do not come to court?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second ברייתא gives a different proof for the same reading.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The number 'two' does not fit litigants, since more than two can come to court

steps.title: The same backup proof from the word 'two'
steps.stepSummary: The second ברייתא adds the same backup גזירה שוה: ״שְׁנֵי״ here matches ״שְׁנֵי עֵדִים״ there.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you are not convinced: it says 'two' here and 'two' there. Just as there it is about witnesses, here too it is about witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: Just like the first ברייתא, this ברייתא adds the גזירה שוה as a backup proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The backup is the same as in Step 7. It works no matter how many litigants can come to court.

keyTerms.meaning: "On the word of two witnesses": the פסוק that 'there' refers to

phrases.english: And if you wish to say otherwise:
it is stated here "two,"
and it is stated there "two";
just as there it is about witnesses,
so too here it is about witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the backup proof to the second ברייתא's argument.

steps.title: Why the backup in the second ברייתא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא again asks what ״אִם נַפְשְׁךָ לוֹמַר״ means here. What is weak about the 'three litigants' proof?
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'if you wish to say' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up its next move. It asks why the second ברייתא's first proof was not enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each ברייתא had a different first proof, so each needs its own explanation of why a backup was added.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'your soul': here it means what you want or are inclined to argue

phrases.english: What is meant by "if you wish to say"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks why the backup proof in Step 11 was needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What weakness in the 'three litigants' proof made the backup necessary

steps.title: 'Two' could mean the plaintiff and the defendant
steps.stepSummary: Someone could argue that 'two' fits litigants after all: a case has two sides, the plaintiff and the defendant. So the ברייתא adds the גזירה שוה, which proves the point anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you would say: the verse is speaking about the plaintiff and the defendant. That is why it says: 'two' here and 'two' there. Just as there it is about witnesses, here too it is about witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the weak spot in the second ברייתא's first proof, and the גזירה שוה settles it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if more people are involved, every case has two sides, a תובע and a נתבע. So 'two' could still describe בעלי דינין, and the 'three people' proof is not airtight. The גזירה שוה settles it: ״שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ are the עדים.

keyTerms.meaning: The plaintiff, the one making the claim
The defendant, the one being claimed against

steps.whatToRemember: Both ברייתות agree that ״וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ is about עדים, so עדים must be 'men.' Each first proof has a weak spot, but the גזירה שוה from ״שְׁנֵי עֵדִים״ backs up both. This is why women are not included in שבועת העדות.
steps.whyThisMatters: The second ברייתא now matches the first in structure: a first proof with a weak spot, backed up by the same גזירה שוה. A third ברייתא follows in the next step with the same pattern.

phrases.english: And if you would say:
the verse is speaking about a plaintiff and a defendant;
therefore: it is stated here "two" and it is stated there "two";

phrases.aramaic: מָה לְהַלָּן בְּעֵדִים אַף כָּאן בְּעֵדִים.
phrases.english: just as there it is about witnesses, so too here it is about witnesses.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: בְּתוֹבֵעַ וְנִתְבָּע קָא מִשְׁתַּעֵי קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 12 by naming the weakness in the 'three litigants' proof.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Two' could mean the two sides of a case, תובע and נתבע, so the גזירה שוה is needed.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: ״שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ refers to עדים, as the גזירה שוה with ״שְׁנֵי עֵדִים״ confirms.

steps.title: A third proof: women also come to court
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא proves that ״שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ means עדים. If it meant בעלי דינין, why say 'men'? Women come to court too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: 'Then the two men shall stand' is talking about witnesses. Do you say witnesses, or maybe litigants? You can answer: is it only men who come to court, and women don't come to court?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third ברייתא that agrees ״שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ means עדים. It gives a new reason: the word 'men'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The step 10 proof was built on the word 'two'. This proof is built on the word 'men'. Women can be בעלי דינין. So a פסוק that only says 'men' cannot be describing litigants. It must be describing עדים, who are men.

phrases.english: Another ברייתא teaches:
"Then the two men shall stand"
the verse is speaking about witnesses.
Do you say it is about witnesses,
or is it only about the litigants?
Can you really say that?
phrases.notes: Literally 'you said'. Here it means: how could you say it's litigants?

phrases.english: Do only men come to court for judgment,
and women do not come to court?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third ברייתא reaches the same conclusion with a different proof ('men' instead of 'two').
steps.raayaSupportSource: Logic: women also come to court as litigants, so 'men' must mean witnesses

steps.title: The backup גזירה שוה again
steps.stepSummary: The third ברייתא adds the same backup: ״שְׁנֵי״ here matches ״שְׁנֵי עֵדִים״ there.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want to say that proof is not good enough: it says 'two' here and 'two' there. Just as there it means witnesses, so too here it means witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: In case the 'women' proof can be pushed aside, the ברייתא adds the same backup גזירה שוה we saw before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same גזירה שוה from steps 7 and 11. 'Two' here is linked to 'two witnesses' in the earlier פסוק. So the point is proven even if the logic proof fails.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish to say (that the first proof is weak)

phrases.english: And if you wish to say that is no proof:
It says here "two"
and it says there "two",
phrases.notes: דברים 19:15, "on the word of two witnesses"

phrases.english: just as there it is about witnesses,
so too here it is about witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a backup proof in case the 'women' argument fails.

steps.title: What is weak about the 'women' proof?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needed ״אִם נַפְשְׁךָ לוֹמַר״ here. What could be wrong with the 'women' proof?
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'if you wish to say' mean here?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks again what weakness the ברייתא is worried about. This sets up the next step's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'women' proof sounds strong. The גמרא wants to know how someone could reject it, since that is why the backup was added.

phrases.english: What does "if you wish to say" mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the backup proof of step 15 was needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What weakness in the 'women' proof made the ברייתא add the גזירה שוה

steps.title: Women usually stay out of court, so 'men' proves nothing
steps.stepSummary: Someone could argue: the פסוק says 'men' only because women do not usually go to court, based on ״כׇּל כְּבוּדָּה בַת מֶלֶךְ פְּנִימָה״. So the ברייתא adds the גזירה שוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say: going to court is not a woman's usual way, because 'All the glory of the king's daughter is within.' So the פסוק just speaks about the usual case, men. That is why the ברייתא adds: it says 'two' here and 'two' there. Just as there it means witnesses, so too here.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the weakness. The פסוק may say 'men' only because that is the common case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Women usually stayed out of public settings like court. So a פסוק about litigants could naturally say 'men'. That means the word 'men' does not prove the פסוק is talking about witnesses. The גזירה שוה proves it anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not her usual way
All the glory of the king's daughter is within

steps.whatToRemember: All three ברייתות agree that ״שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ means עדים. Each gives a different first proof, and each backs it up with the same גזירה שוה from ״שְׁנֵי עֵדִים״.

phrases.english: And if you would say:
it is not a woman's usual way to go to court,
because of "All the glory of the king's daughter is within";
so: it says here "two"
and it says there "two",
just as there it is about witnesses,
so too here it is about witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק may say 'men' only because women usually do not go to court, so the גזירה שוה is needed.

steps.title: Litigants must stand
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא learns from ״וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ that בעלי דינין have a מצוה to stand in court.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: 'Then the two men shall stand' teaches that it is a מצוה for the litigants to stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It brings a ברייתא that reads the same פסוק as a rule about בעלי דינין: they must stand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the word 'stand' is the focus, not who the 'two men' are. This ברייתא reads the פסוק as talking about the litigants and learns that they stand during the case.
steps.confusionAlert: Just before this, the פסוק was read as talking about עדים. This ברייתא uses the same פסוק to teach about בעלי דינין. It is a different teaching from the same words.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
"Then the two men shall stand"
it is a מצוה for the litigants to stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic based on the same פסוק: how litigants are treated in court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בעלי דינין must stand during the court case.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: both may sit, but they must be equal
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says the court may seat both בעלי דינין. What is forbidden is treating them unequally: one stands while the other sits, or one speaks freely while the other is cut short.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said: I heard that if the judges want to seat both of them, they may. So what is forbidden? That one should stand and the other sit, or that one may say all he needs while the judge tells the other, 'Cut your words short.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with the first opinion. Standing is not required. The real rule is equality.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, the problem is not sitting. It is unequal treatment. Both may stand or both may sit, and both must get the same chance to speak.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said: I heard
that if they wished to seat both of them,
they may seat them;
so what is forbidden?

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא אֶחָד עוֹמֵד וְאֶחָד יוֹשֵׁב,
phrases.english: that one should not be standing while the other sits,
or one says all that he needs to say
while to the other the judge says, "Cut your words short."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A disagreeing opinion: standing is not required, only equal treatment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both litigants may be seated. What is forbidden is unequal treatment in posture or in time to speak.

steps.title: Equal treatment learned from ״בְּצֶדֶק תִּשְׁפֹּט עֲמִיתֶךָ״
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא learns the equality rule from ״בְּצֶדֶק תִּשְׁפֹּט עֲמִיתֶךָ״: no sitting for one and standing for the other, and no giving one more time to speak.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: 'In righteousness you shall judge your fellow' means that one should not sit while the other stands, or one say all he needs while the judge tells the other, 'Cut your words short.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק that is the source for the equal-treatment rule רבי יהודה just described.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Judging 'in righteousness' includes how the court treats each side, not only the final ruling. Unequal posture or unequal speaking time is not fair judgment.

keyTerms.meaning: In righteousness you shall judge your fellow

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
"In righteousness you shall judge your fellow"

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא אֶחָד יוֹשֵׁב וְאֶחָד עוֹמֵד,
phrases.english: that one should not be sitting while the other stands,
or one says all that he needs to say
while to the other the judge says: "Cut your words short."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a פסוק as the source for the equal-treatment rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The judge must treat both litigants equally in posture and in time to speak.

steps.title: Another reading: judge others favorably
steps.stepSummary: A second reading of ״בְּצֶדֶק תִּשְׁפֹּט עֲמִיתֶךָ״: always judge your fellow favorably.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: 'In righteousness you shall judge your fellow' means: judge your friend favorably.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a second meaning of the same פסוק. Every person should give others the benefit of the doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This reading takes 'judge' beyond the courtroom. When someone's action could be seen in a good way or a bad way, you should see it in the good way.

keyTerms.meaning: Favorably; giving the benefit of the doubt

steps.whatToRemember: ״בְּצֶדֶק תִּשְׁפֹּט עֲמִיתֶךָ״ teaches two things: judges must treat both sides equally, and every person should judge others favorably.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the well-known source for the מצוה of דן לכף זכות, judging others favorably, which applies to everyone and not just to judges.

phrases.english: Another explanation:
"In righteousness you shall judge your fellow"

phrases.aramaic: הֱוֵי דָּן אֶת חֲבֵירְךָ לְכַף זְכוּת.
phrases.english: judge your friend favorably.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, broader meaning of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person must judge his fellow favorably.

steps.title: רב יוסף: judge a fellow in תורה 'nicely'
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף reads עֲמִיתֶךָ as 'the one who is with you in תורה and מצוות' and teaches that such a person should be judged 'nicely.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף taught: 'In righteousness shall you judge your fellow.' Someone who is with you in תורה and מצוות, try to judge him nicely.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף gives a new reading of the same פסוק from the last two steps. He says it speaks about how to treat a fellow Torah scholar in court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He splits the word עֲמִיתֶךָ into עִם שֶׁאִתְּךָ, 'the one who is with you,' meaning with you in תורה and מצוות. The words 'judge him nicely' are vague. They cannot mean bending the law, and the story that follows explains what they do mean.

keyTerms.meaning: Your fellow; here read as 'the one with you'
The one who is with you

steps.confusionAlert: 'Judge him nicely' does NOT mean ruling in his favor. The story right after this shows it is about honor, not about the outcome of the case.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef teaches:
"In righteousness shall you judge your fellow" –
one who is with you in Torah and in מצוות,
phrases.notes: He hears the word עֲמִיתֶךָ as two words: עִם שֶׁאִתְּךָ, 'the one who is with you.'

phrases.english: try to judge him nicely.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third reading of the same פסוק, after the readings about equal treatment and judging favorably.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A litigant who is a fellow in תורה and מצוות should be judged 'nicely.'

steps.title: רב יוסף sends a note about רב עולא's case
steps.stepSummary: רב עולא had a case before רב נחמן, and רב יוסף sent רב נחמן a message calling רב עולא a fellow in תורה and מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עולא, son of רב עילאי, had a court case before רב נחמן. רב יוסף sent him a message: 'עולא our friend is a fellow in תורה and מצוות.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story that applies רב יוסף's teaching to a real case. This step sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף's message uses the very word עָמִית from the פסוק. In effect he is telling רב נחמן, 'apply the rule I just taught.' What that request actually means is not yet clear.

phrases.english: Rav Ulla, son of Rav Ilai,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה לֵיהּ דִּינָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן.
phrases.english: had a court case before Rav Naḥman.
Rav Yosef sent to him:
Ulla our friend is a fellow in Torah and in מצוות.
phrases.notes: He is pointing to the פסוק he just taught: 'judge your fellow in righteousness.'

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב עוּלָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב עִילַּאי הֲוָה לֵיהּ דִּינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Puts רב יוסף's teaching into a real court case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יוסף asks רב נחמן to treat רב עולא as an עָמִית in תורה and מצוות.

steps.title: רב נחמן: am I supposed to favor him?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן is puzzled: why send me this? Surely I am not supposed to show him favoritism!
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: Why did he send me this? To flatter him?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן asks what רב יוסף's message could possibly mean. He rejects the idea that he should tilt the case toward רב עולא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taken at face value, the message could sound like a request to favor a scholar. That would break the basic rule that every judgment must be fair. So רב נחמן assumes the message must mean something else.

phrases.english: He said: For what did he send to me?
To flatter him?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions what רב יוסף's message in Step 23 is asking for.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does 'judge him nicely' require, if not favoritism?

steps.title: The answer: hear his case first
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן concludes that the message means he should start with רב עולא's case before the others.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then he said: He sent it so that I would begin with his case.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers his own question. 'Judging nicely' means giving the scholar the honor of having his case heard first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The honor shown to a תלמיד חכם is about order, not outcome. His case goes first in line, but the ruling itself stays completely fair.

keyTerms.meaning: Then he said again (changing his view)

steps.whatToRemember: A תלמיד חכם gets priority in the order of cases, but never a different verdict.
steps.whyThisMatters: This defines 'judge him nicely' in a way that does not clash with the equality rules learned just before.

phrases.english: He then said:
to open with his dispute,
phrases.notes: He means: if several cases are waiting, take רב עולא's case first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in Step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The message asks for priority in hearing the case, not favoritism in the ruling.
